newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Boeing makes progress in merger talks with EU.
newsitem.headline: Boeing makes progress in merger talks with EU.

text.p: Boeing Co. said Monday it had made progress in weekend talks with the European Commission on its planned $14 billion acquisition of McDonnell Douglas Corp.
"We have not reached a final agreement ... We are not there yet," James Frank, Boeing's European executive vice president for government and public affairs, said.
"We made progress," he added. "We still are optimistic that we will find a mutually acceptable solution."
While Frank said progress had been made on the issue of what changes to the deal were needed to win European Union approval, he declined to say whether Beoing had offered further concessions.
"I'm not prepared to say," Frank said.
EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert has made clear the deal could not be approved without Boeing offering "structural" changes to address EU antitrust concerns.
The U.S. Federal Trade Commission has already cleared the merger.

There was no immediate word from the Commission on the weekend talks. But a Commission source said last Thursday that the EU executive remained confident that Boeing would come up with adequate changes to the planned deal to meet EU concerns.
The Commission is due to decide July 23 whether to approve the merger. However, legally the Commission has until the end of July.
Frank said the weekend talks had been with the Commission's merger task force, and Boeing hoped the discussions would continue, but he gave no details.
The FTC cleared the deal with no conditions July 1, saying McDonnell's commercial aircraft operation was no longer a viable stand-alone business.
The FTC also hinted it could live with some EU action against Boeing's exclusive aircraft supply deals with several airlines.

Commission thinking, backed on July 4 by antitrust officials from EU national capitals, is that McDonnell's assets are nevertheless valuable to a merged company and that Boeing should offer some remedy in return for EU approval.
The Commission has the power to review corporate deals where the firms involved have a combined worldwide revenues of at least $5.5 billion and the EU revenue of each firm amounts to $278 million.
The European Commission argues that the merger would add to Boeing's already dominant position in the aircraft industry.

Its figures say the deal would give the merged firms a 70 percent share of the market for large civil aircraft -- those with more than 100 seats. This compares with 30 percent for its rival Airbus Industrie, a four-nation European consortium.
Among its other concerns, it opposes Boeing's exclusive contracts to supply aircraft to airlines such as Delta, American and Continental.
It also worries about the possibility of spillovers of government money, earmarked for research and development in defence, into Boeing's civil aviation business.
